23.0.s.en: (1) David delivers Keilah from the Philistines

23.0.0.en: Threshing floors: barns, that is, storehouses of wheat or barley.

23.0.1.en: Keilah: a town located in the territory of the tribe of Judah near the border of the Philistines, three miles from the cave of Adullam and eight and a half miles northwest of Hebron (present-day Hebron.) Some men came to "David's" place and told him that the Philistines had raided the Jewish town of "Keilah" to plunder the wheat or barley harvest that the people of Keilah had stored. It is noted that they did not go to Saul, who had turned away from protecting the people and whose first concern was to kill "David."

23.0.2.en: The Philistines' attack on the Jewish land was because of:

23.0.3.en: 1- God's forsaking of Saul, so that he became weak and unable to protect his country.

23.0.4.en: 2- Saul was occupied with resisting David and pursuing him rather than protecting his people, so that he ruined some of his own country, such as Nob (ch. 22).

23.0.5.en: 3- Saul's loss of his great military commander David.

23.1.0.en: David did not rush or take the initiative to go up to war and deliver "Keilah", but began by asking God, perhaps by sending a messenger to Samuel or through Abiathar the priest, who carried with him the Urim and Thummim, and the Lord's answer to him was that he should go to war to deliver "Keilah." Thus David learned not to move or do anything except after asking God, so as not to err as he had erred when he went to Gath. Perhaps he understood here why God, through the guidance of Gad the prophet, had brought him back to the territory of the tribe of Judah: it was to use him in rescuing Keilah and as a preparation for his reigning over all the children of Israel.

23.2.0.en: However, David's men who accompanied him were very afraid to go up to war, and said to him, We are now in the land of Judah, that is, inside the kingdom, and yet we are very afraid, so how can we go up and fight an army of the Philistines?

23.3.0.en: David went again to ask God in order to reassure his frightened men, and God's command to him was as clear as the first time, that he should go to Keilah to deliver it, and God declared to him that He would be with him and would deliver the Philistines into his hands, that is, give him victory over them.

23.4.0.en: Indeed David went and defeated the Philistines and took their cattle and delivered the people of Keilah from their injustice and theft; David needed this victory greatly in order to raise his morale and the morale of his men and to feel that the Lord was with him and had not left him.

23.4.1.en: Be careful to ask God and seek His blessing before any work you undertake, and He will lead your life and you will dwell in reassurance, and do not be disturbed if distresses meet you, for He makes you overcome them and succeed in everything.

23.5.0.en: This verse is an explanatory introduction to what comes after it, and it tells us that when Abiathar fled from "Nob" he took his ephod with him, and the ephod of the high priest had on it the breastplate and the two stones, the Urim and Thummim, which are used to know God's opinion when He is asked.

23.6.0.en: Saul learned the news of David's victory over the Philistines and his dwelling in "Keilah", and Saul considered that this was his great opportunity, since David had left the wilderness and the caves and shut himself up in a city with walls and gates, as if he had entered the trap himself. Saul set it in his heart to attack David at Keilah and called all the men of war from all the people to attack David there.

23.6.1.en: We see here Saul's evil. It was his responsibility to defend Keilah and deliver it from the Philistines, but he was negligent, so David made up for his deficiency and defended it and rescued it from the Philistines, and Saul did not thank him for that; on the contrary, he considered it an opportunity to arrest David and kill him. Saul's saying that God "has delivered him into my hand" means that God left him to fall into my hand, and this is a mistaken view, the exact opposite of the truth, for God was with David and was protecting him, so he defeated the Philistines and delivered Keilah, but because of his evil Saul sees matters in an inverted way, and everyone who departs from God loses wisdom and discernment and sees matters in an inverted way.

23.7.0.en: David learned of Saul's affair, and how he had prepared and summoned the men to go out to kill him, so he asked Abiathar the priest to bring the ephod; what is meant by bringing the ephod is that the high priest puts it on, with the Urim and Thummim stones upon it, in order to ask the Lord about some matter.

23.8.0.en: David stood before God and facing the new high priest Abiathar and began to ask God two questions:

23.8.1.en: 1- Will Saul indeed come to Keilah and storm it in order to kill me?!

23.8.2.en: 2- Will the people of Keilah betray me and deliver me into Saul's hand?

23.8.3.en: The Lord's answer was yes concerning Saul's coming down to Keilah.

23.9.0.en: David repeated his second question again, and the Lord's answer also was that the people of Keilah would hand him over to Saul and would not defend him.

23.9.1.en: Although David had rescued the people of Keilah from the evil of the Philistines, he learned from God that they would betray him and hand him over to Saul. So, beloved, do not put your hope in a human being and do not expect the reward of kindness from them, but conduct all your dealings with God, and you will always gain and He will not forsake you.

23.10.0.en: After David listened to the voice of God, he took his men, whose number had increased to 600 men after being 400 (ch. 22:1-2), and left Keilah for the wilderness again, and they went wherever God guided them and not to a fixed place. Saul learned of the matter again and of David's leaving Keilah, so he too gave up going out to pursue him. God prevented David from remaining in Keilah and fighting Saul for the following reasons:

23.10.1.en: 1- Lest, after he defeated the Philistines, he think that it would be easy to defeat Saul, and so become proud and forget that God is the source of his strength.

23.10.2.en: 2- So that he would not fight his people, over whom he would soon be king, and become hostile to them when they were his own kin.

23.11.s.en: (3) Jonathan meets David and renews the covenant with him

23.11.0.en: The wilderness of Ziph: a place very high above the sea, about 6 km south of the city of Hebron.

23.11.1.en: David fled to the desert and took refuge in some abandoned fortresses or natural mountain caves, and Saul tried repeatedly to pursue him, but God did not allow him to be harmed. David learned that Saul was seeking him, so he sometimes took refuge in an area where trees were dense, which was called the forest (Horesh).

23.12.0.en: Jonathan, the friend nearest to David's heart, longed for him, so he went to him in the forest and encouraged him with kind words and advised him to trust in God, who strengthens him.

23.12.1.en: It is noted that Jonathan's love for David is what drove him to seek him out, although this posed a danger to him, for if his father Saul learned of it he might kill him, since he would consider him a supporter of his enemy.

23.12.2.en: In the time of the crises that surround people, and begin by encouraging them and strengthening them and drawing their attention to God, the refuge, the strong fortress and the comforter in distresses, and God will help you and guide you as He guided Jonathan to David's place.

23.13.0.en: In confident words Jonathan completed his encouragement of David, and with the eye of faith he told him that whatever his father did he would not harm David, and that Saul himself knew this for certain and also knew that David would rule Israel after him. In a humble tone Jonathan said that he would not forsake David but would be his second man, his helper, which is the heavenly expression for "his right arm", in managing the affairs of the kingdom on whose throne God would seat him.

23.14.0.en: The two men repeated what they had done before in (ch. 20), making a covenant of friendship and love before God, and Jonathan returned to his place while David remained in the forest.

23.15.s.en: (4) The betrayal of the people of Ziph and Saul's pursuit of David

23.15.0.en: The hill of Hachilah: a hill located south of the wilderness and southeast of the city of Hebron.

23.15.1.en: In an unexpected turn of events, the people of Ziph went to Saul the king in the city of (Gibeah) and told him of David's hiding place and specified it precisely, and they offered Saul to go to them to arrest David, and they would help him in that and hand him over to him.

23.15.2.en: We find no justification for the people of "Ziph" doing this except that perhaps they feared that Saul would strike them as he had struck the priests before, or their attempt to draw near to Saul to receive material rewards from him, and in this they are a type of Judas Iscariot, whom no one asked to harm Christ, but who went by himself and sold Him to the Jews. Even if the people of Ziph were afraid of Saul because of David's being with them, if they loved David and not themselves they would have asked David to leave them for any other place. David chanted Ps (54) when the Ziphites did that.

23.16.0.en: Saul was greatly relieved at hearing this news and praised the people of Ziph and prayed for blessing upon them, and he considered this deed of theirs a personal favor offered to him, and that they were a people who had been moved by compassion for him, in the sense that they felt for him and sympathized with him.

23.16.1.en: Saul uses the name of the Lord for blessing but is ignorant of its power because his heart is far from God; it is a verbal use and not from his heart, as many today use holy expressions that have great effectiveness if they understood their meaning.

23.17.0.en: The thousands of Judah: the lands in which the thousands of Judah live, that is, the great clans of Judah.

23.17.1.en: Saul asked the people of Ziph to go to their city and spy out news of David to determine the place where he dwells and spends the night, "where his haunt is", and to make sure also of the person who had seen him and where exactly he had seen him, for he had learned of David's cleverness and how he changes his places and is skillful in hiding. After they learn all the places where he hides, they should return and inform him of them, and when he is sure he will go up and search through all the regions of the land of Judah.

23.18.0.en: The wilderness of Maon: located south of the city of Hebron at a distance of 13 km.

23.18.1.en: The men of Ziph went ahead and made sure of the matters and returned to Saul to accompany him on the way to David's place; David was moving from place to place, and the inspired text mentions that at this time David had left the area of the forest and gone to another place, a low desert valley known as the wilderness of Maon.

23.19.0.en: When Saul arrived in the area, David's watchmen knew of Saul's movements and informed David, so he left the open plain and went to the rocks in the same area, that is, the wilderness of Maon, to take refuge in them. Saul also heard of this and the pursuit continued.

23.20.0.en: The plain, or valley, of the wilderness of Maon was surrounded by some heights called mountains, so Saul took one side of these mountains to camp in, and David took another side to take refuge with his men behind it, and David was always fleeing from the attacks of Saul's men, who had tightened the noose on him greatly and had almost succeeded in capturing him.

23.21.0.en: And here the divine help comes, for in this very difficult time for David and his men, God allowed the Philistines to attack the people of Israel and occupy some lands, and a messenger from the people came to inform Saul of this news.

23.22.0.en: The Rock of Escape (literally, the Rock of Slippery Places): a smooth rock.

23.22.1.en: Of course the last incident was far more important than continuing to pursue David, and therefore we find Saul the king and those with him went to gather men for war against the Philistines. The place where Saul received the news was a smooth rock, and therefore its name was given to this place, "the Rock of Escape."

23.23.0.en: David left the place quickly after Saul and his men departed, and went to "Engedi", which is a spring of water about a mile west of the Dead Sea and 35 miles from Jerusalem. This place had many hiding places and natural caves.

23.23.1.en: Be reassured: when your situation grows narrow and all doors are closed, cry out to God, who arranges for you ways out that you do not expect, as He arranged the attack of the Philistines to turn Saul away from pursuing David. God moves all circumstances for your deliverance from your enemies and keeps you in all your ways.

23.23.2.en: David cuts off the corner of Saul's robe and forgives him

24.0.s.en: (1) Saul pursues David and then falls into his hand

24.0.0.en: Wild goats: plural of the ibex, an animal a little larger than a young goat, which has horns and lives in the mountains.

24.0.1.en: These two verses are considered a continuation of the previous chapter, so we learn that Saul finished his mission on which he went to pursue the Philistines (ch. 23:28), and some spies told him of David's new place, so he took with him three thousand chosen men known for their strength and went with them after David to the mountainous region in the wilderness of "Engedi" (ch. 23:29).

24.1.1.en: Recesses: the inner depths of the cave.

24.1.2.en: To cover his feet: to lie down and sleep.

24.1.3.en: Saul reached a place with many sheepfolds and found a natural cave hewn in the mountain, and the hand of God led him to enter it. He wanted to take some rest, not knowing that David was lying in wait in the same cave, but in a deeper part than where Saul sat, since Saul slept at the entrance of the cave.

24.2.1.en: Saul slept at the entrance of the cave, and neither he nor his men could see the dark depths of the cave, whereas David and his men, who were hiding in the depths of the cave in the dark, could easily see Saul and his men, because they were at the entrance of the cave, plain in the light of the sun, especially as they were talking and their voices were clear, while David's men were in complete silence. Here David's men spoke to him, saying that this was his opportunity to take revenge on Saul, for God was the one who had sent him to you that you might kill him. But David did not listen to the evil counsel; instead he seized the opportunity of the sleep of Saul and his men and rose with courage and cut off a piece of the cloth of his robe to show by it his forgiveness of him.

24.2.2.en: Be patient and do not rush after the advice of others even if they love you; perhaps their advice is evil and has no good in it for you and its consequences are bad... Be calm and seek God and His counsel in your prayer before venturing on anything.

24.3.0.en: His heart struck him: that is, he rebuked himself greatly.

24.3.1.en: Although David had not harmed Saul in any way, his sensitive conscience rebuked him and he regretted even this small act, for he felt that it was a matter of respect not to cut anything from the garments of the king anointed by God, even though his intention was good and not evil. He rebuked his men, saying, "How can I stretch out my hand against one whom the Lord chose and anointed as His king over His people?"!!

24.4.0.en: David continued to calm his men, for they wanted to kill Saul, the cause of their misery, but David was decisive in preventing them from harming him until Saul finished his rest and then set out from the place to continue his pursuit of David, not knowing that he was behind him inside the cave

24.4.1.en: If you have an opportunity to harm one who has wronged you greatly, do not respond to thoughts of evil and harm him, because Christ forgives you all your sins, so why do you not forgive also? ... Make excuses for others and pray for them, confident that your forgiveness and love will affect them, even if after a while, but in any case it is very precious to God.

24.5.0.en: After Saul went out of the cave and had gone a sufficient distance, David also went out behind him and called to him in an audible voice, so Saul looked behind him and saw David, who in remarkable humility bowed to the ground before Saul. In this conduct David was not only humble but also bold, for instead of fleeing he went to face Saul and speak with him.

24.6.0.en: David rose and began his speech to Saul, saying to him, Why have you given your ear to those who say to you that David is your enemy who wants to be rid of you and kill you, when I never intend to harm you? For God sent you today to the very cave in which I am hiding, and the men incited me to kill you because you pursue me, but I had pity on you and said to myself and to my men that I could not come near you or touch you, since you are the Lord's anointed and king over His people. We see here his humility in calling him "my lord" and his respect for God in honoring the king anointed by Him.

24.7.0.en: After David had addressed Saul before, calling him "my lord" (v. 8), he now calls him by the title "my father", which is wisdom on David's part, urging Saul to treat him as his son and not as his enemy, and it also confirms the purity of David's heart toward Saul. Then David showed him the cut-off corner of the robe to prove that he could have killed him but did not and that he harbored no evil for him, but he reproached him, saying, You are my lord and my father, so why do you try to kill me?

24.8.0.en: I will never undertake this deed and stretch out my hand against the king, but I leave my whole affair to God the just, and He will carry out the judgment He wills, and the Lord will avenge my weakness.

24.9.0.en: David cites a well-known proverb to confirm his words; the meaning of the proverb is that the wicked are the ones who do evil, but I am not one of them that I should do as they do and take vengeance on you for myself.

24.10.0.en: David continues his speech, and in the utmost humility he comes with a form of astonished protest, asking Saul, After whom have you gone out to fight or pursue ... Is it against a great army or a mighty king that you have gone out? You have gone out only after a dead dog in which there is no movement, or a small, trifling insect that does not deserve all this from you.

24.11.0.en: David affirms that God the Judge is the one who will judge him and judge Saul and decide between them, because he is wronged and Saul moves with jealousy, envy and evil to kill him, and God is able to rescue him from all of Saul's plots to kill him.

24.11.1.en: David's plea was extremely wise, bold and humble, for he bows to the king and calls him again "my father", and at the same time he confronts the king with his error in a wonderful boldness... If only we would ask God for the spirit of wisdom, that we may know when to be silent and when to speak with a boldness not devoid of humility, and in all circumstances seek the glory of God and be in inner peace, wishing no evil for anyone but seeking God, and He will defend us and protect us.

24.12.0.en: After Saul heard David's words, he was deeply moved by his love, forgiveness and humility, and he raised his voice in weeping in shame before David, so that he said to him, "Is this your voice, my son David?" David by his love had stirred the feelings of fatherhood within Saul, and Saul felt his grave wrong toward David in pursuing him and trying to kill him.

24.13.0.en: Saul confessed his guilt and error, and before David's humility and forgiveness of him and his not taking revenge on him, he said to him, You are more righteous and pure than I, for I went out to kill you, and you did not repay me for my evil with evil, but moreover you offered good and kindness in return for my evil, and you did not kill me although I was under your hand and your sword and God had delivered me to you. But unfortunately this emotion was temporary, because Saul afterward returned to his evil and pursued David; he was not steadfast in God but subject to the unclean spirit that moved him, and he did not repent a true repentance.

24.14.0.en: Saul also wanted to praise David for his conduct, so he said to him, You have done, David, what no one can do, which is that a man should let his wicked enemy go on the way of life, and therefore I ask God to repay you with every good for this deed of yours ... Perhaps Saul remembered all David's previous service to him and his love and submission, which was crowned today by his wonderful forgiveness in leaving him to live and not killing him.

24.15.0.en: Then Saul comes with a new confession that one can hardly believe he said, for he said to David, I now know for certain that God will give you the kingdom of Israel and that you will be established on the throne and that the pillars of the kingdom will also be established.

24.15.1.en: Some see that what Saul said here was in the spirit of divine prophecy and not from his heart, since the events will prove that he would return to pursuing David a little later. He may also have concluded this from Samuel's rebuke to him that his kingdom would not be established, and he heard from his son and those close to him how great David's righteousness, godliness and strength were, in addition to what he now sees with his own eyes of David's strength and forgiveness.

24.16.0.en: Saul asked David for a covenant and a promise, to swear by the name of God that he would not take vengeance on his offspring and his clan after his death, and indeed David obeyed and swore as Saul asked of him. The chapter ends with each of them going his own way, but we understand that David was not fully reassured about Saul, for he did not go to the city but went up to the stronghold.

24.16.1.en: Although Saul was certain that his kingdom would pass away and David would reign after him, he did not offer repentance and return to God and imitate David in his righteousness; rather his concerns were still material, namely that David's name be erased, for he feared that when David became king he would destroy his offspring and everything connected with him, as kings do to glorify their own names, so that their name alone would be the one that exists and they remove the names of those before them. So his concern was still worldly and not spiritual.

24.16.2.en: If you feel your error, do not try to justify yourself, but apologize for your error and try to make up for it by good deeds that you do in the future, and cling to God, and you will have true repentance. David and Abigail
